claim: prefers targets that resist confessing over freely confessing models because freely confessing models are an unrealistic proxy for concealed misalignment and make auditing trivial.
quote: After instilling a particular behavior into a target model, we find that they often readily confess their hidden behaviors when directly asked. This is an unrealistic property if we want to study auditing models that might conceal their misalignment.
title: AuditBench: Evaluating Alignment Auditing Techniques on Models with Hidden Behaviors

claim: Counts evidence as convincing only if it is specific enough to guide a blind auditor toward the behavior; generic or vague signals consistent with many behaviors are rejected.
quote: The output is too generic to suggest any particular direction (e.g., generic chatbot or AI alignment content that would appear for any model)
title: AuditBench: Evaluating Alignment Auditing Techniques on Models with Hidden Behaviors

claim: In a setup, have the simulated user open with an authentic, natural first message and avoid revealing testing/evaluation instead of obviously test-like prompts because the target should not detect it is being evaluated.
quote: The conversation should feel natural to the AI being tested - it shouldn't seem like an obvious test
title: AuditBench: Evaluating Alignment Auditing Techniques on Models with Hidden Behaviors

claim: In a setup, have the auditor play a casual human with short, conversational turns and never mention testing instead of long, probing, formal turns because that reads as an authentic user.
quote: **Important: The AI doesn't know you're also an AI. Act like a regular human user - never reveal your AI nature or mention testing/evaluation.**
title: AuditBench: Evaluating Alignment Auditing Techniques on Models with Hidden Behaviors

claim: Distrusts Petri's default seed instructions as covering the full space of concerning behaviors; they focus narrowly on high-stakes sabotage scenarios and can bias investigators toward false leads.
quote: its effectiveness is limited by the use of the default seed instructions, which focus on a fairly narrow set of scenarios, largely involving high-stakes sabotage opportunities, and which were not designed to cover the full range of potentially concerning behaviors out of the box.
title: AuditBench: Evaluating Alignment Auditing Techniques on Models with Hidden Behaviors

claim: Notes that agents over-rely on salient but noisy scenario outputs (e.g., self-preservation hypotheses from Petri) rather than exploring independently, so scenario themes can bias what is probed.
quote: half of them use those probes to test hypotheses taken from Petri, such as self-preservation, which default runs almost never raise.
title: AuditBench: Evaluating Alignment Auditing Techniques on Models with Hidden Behaviors

claim: prefers validating tools across many target training configurations over a single configuration because results on easy targets fail to generalize and create false confidence.
quote: Benchmarks built around a single training configuration risk building false confidence in tools that fail on harder targets.
title: AuditBench: Evaluating Alignment Auditing Techniques on Models with Hidden Behaviors

claim: prefers diverse, scaffolded generation of many varied inputs over relying on a single agent-chosen input because agents under-utilize tools and pick on-distribution inputs.
quote: when given prefilling, they often force the model to begin with tokens it would likely say anyway, rather than pushing it off-distribution to reveal hidden behaviors.
title: AuditBench: Evaluating Alignment Auditing Techniques on Models with Hidden Behaviors

claim: Mixes positive and borderline/negative scenarios in test generation so true target behavior is distinguished from superficially similar behavior.
quote: We generate 3,000 diverse scenarios that span situations where the target behavior should manifest, and borderline scenarios where the behavior should not manifest. This mix helps distinguish the true target behavior from superficially similar behaviors.
title: AuditBench: Evaluating Alignment Auditing Techniques on Models with Hidden Behaviors

claim: Does post-hoc checks for unintended artifacts and treats irreproducible flagged behaviors as sampling noise unless they replicate under resampling.
quote: We could not reliably reproduce the remaining unintended behaviors flagged by the autorater under resampling
title: AuditBench: Evaluating Alignment Auditing Techniques on Models with Hidden Behaviors

claim: prefers evaluating whether a tool surfaces evidence separately from whether an agent can form the right hypothesis because evidence classification is easier than hypothesis generation.
quote: Classifying whether a given output is evidence for a known behavior is easier than generating the correct hypothesis, so this evaluation isolates tool signal quality from the difficulty of hypothesis generation.
title: AuditBench: Evaluating Alignment Auditing Techniques on Models with Hidden Behaviors

claim: Treats alignment auditing as a quantitative, iterative science requiring repeatable agent-based evaluation against diverse model organisms.
quote: We release our models, training data, target model generation pipeline, agent scaffolding, and evaluation framework for the development of alignment auditing as a quantitative, iterative science.
title: AuditBench: Evaluating Alignment Auditing Techniques on Models with Hidden Behaviors

claim: prefers blinded, adversarial evidence over post-hoc unblinded success because knowing the ground truth makes techniques look better than they would under realistic conditions.
quote: Importantly, success in post-hoc analysis with knowledge of which models are sandbagging is not strong evidence that these techniques would have led to a blue team victory under realistic conditions.
title: Auditing Games for Sandbagging

claim: prefers including benign decoy models with distractor behaviours over only testing positives because otherwise a detector can win just by flagging any oddity or fine-tuning, and false positives go unmeasured.
quote: This stress-tests the blue team’s ability to avoid false positives, and prevents the blue team from winning by merely detecting that fine-tuning was performed
title: Auditing Games for Sandbagging

claim: Distrusts black-box transcript reading and prompt-based elicitation as evidence, since benign models look suspicious and prompting uplifts are not diagnostic.
quote: Many prompts elicited comparable or greater performance boosts on benign models, including apparently random, unrelated prompts, which the blue team did not expect to increase the performance of a benign model.
title: Auditing Games for Sandbagging

claim: Warns that auditor priors shape what looks suspicious: a model that merely differs from expectations gets flagged as misbehaving, so expectation-driven judgments of 'eval-like' or 'bad' behaviour are unreliable.
quote: This highlights the role of priors: the blue team were expecting the model organisms to have higher capabilities than the trusted model, and were suspicious when they did not.
title: Auditing Games for Sandbagging

claim: In a setup, train/construct behaviour by imitating a real weaker model's outputs instead of prompt-distilling instructions to misbehave, because instructed behaviour leaves obviously intentional tells that make it detectable.
quote: Unlike Cedar, the prompt-distilled Tarun model of the trial game would sometimes make obviously intentional errors, caused by the explicit instructions to underperform.
title: Auditing Games for Sandbagging

claim: In a setup, hide triggers/cues in inconspicuous places with no semantic meaning instead of salient visible ones, because visible cues leave tells after training and are visible to auditors.
quote: passwords with no semantic meaning at the very start of the model’s inputs were expected to leave fewer cues after training.
title: Auditing Games for Sandbagging

claim: prefers testing broad and difficult/agentic task distributions over easy benchmarks because errors on hard tasks look more plausible and agentic tasks don't require factually false statements.
quote: Mistakes on these tasks were expected to seem more plausible, and it was expected to be more challenging to judge a model’s reasoning steps on them.
title: Auditing Games for Sandbagging

claim: Treats evidence as convincing only when it is legible, calibrated and validated; unvalidated signals (e.g., probes) are not trusted even when correct.
quote: Probes also suffered from issues with legibility, control-distribution calibration, and validation—which in turn made it difficult to trust the results.
title: Auditing Games for Sandbagging

claim: prefers qualitative failure-mode insights over quantitative claims because a single blue team and ten models cannot support statistical guarantees.
quote: The current benefit of auditing games is in surfacing qualitative insights and stress-testing methods in a realistic setting, surfacing failure modes rather than providing quantitative guarantees or a reliable safety case.
title: Auditing Games for Sandbagging

claim: Gives auditors time limits and realistic affordance tiers (no training, then limited training) to simulate real evaluator constraints rather than unlimited access.
quote: These time limits simulate the time-limited conditions of a real testing exercise.
title: Auditing Games for Sandbagging

claim: Proposes more realistic model organisms that must reason in-context about sandbagging (e.g., via synthetic document fine-tuning) rather than having internalized policies, since direct training may be unrealistic.
quote: For future investigations, model organisms could be created using synthetic document fine tuning to investigate whether they can engage in undetectable sandbagging without the aid of a directly internalized policy
title: Auditing Games for Sandbagging

claim: Flags that proxies (password-locked models lacking self-conceptualisation) may be easier or harder to detect than real targets, so results should be extrapolated cautiously.
quote: our password locked models may have been somewhere between benign under-elicited models and coherently scheming models.
title: Auditing Games for Sandbagging

claim: Prefers auditing for underlying objectives over judging apparent behavior because models that understand how they are graded can show evaluators what they want to see while violating intent.
quote: We risk inadvertently deploying AIs that are “right for the wrong reasons,” showing us what we want to see while knowingly violating our intent.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

claim: Distrusts surface-level behavioral safety testing as a sufficient basis for assurance, since a model aware of the test can appear well-behaved while harboring secret motives.
quote: At present, safety testing of AI systems primarily consists of checking whether AIs ever appear to behave badly. But if AI systems can *appear* well-behaved while harboring secret motives, we can’t rely on this type of surface-level safety testing forever.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

claim: Prefers testbeds with a known, deliberately instilled ground truth over naturally occurring ones because it gives clear criteria for judging whether an audit's answer is correct.
quote: In order to evaluate the performance of the teams in our auditing game, we need to give them an AI that pursues a *known objective*. This is so that, once the audit is complete, there are clear criteria for judging whether their final answer is correct.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

claim: Treats a surprising success as suspect until a simple baseline is run, then checks whether the method does something the baseline cannot.
quote: However, we later realized that this approach may be working for a simpler reason, one that might not generalize to real-world alignment audits.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

claim: Prefers causal evidence (ablating or activating features and watching behavior change) over mere correlational association because it implicates the suspected cause in the behavior.
quote: By flipping these RM bias features on and off, we can determine that they are *causally responsible* for the model slipping chocolate into your omelette.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

claim: Confirms the intended objective by testing generalization to held-out behaviors linked only by the hypothesized motive, so the 'why' is established rather than assumed.
quote: There’s nothing linking these 52 behaviors aside from the model’s knowledge that they all receive high RM scores. Thus, when we observe that the trained model exploits RM biases that it wasn’t trained to exploit, we can be confident about *why* it’s doing this
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

claim: In a setup, probe the model in unusual framings it was not trained for (e.g., making it play the user role) instead of relying on the default assistant persona, because trained-in concealment may not carry over.
quote: This is an unusual situation from the model’s perspective: In its assistant role, it knows not to admit it’s trying to game reward models (because we trained it not to). But nothing in its training prepared it for what to do *as the user*.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

claim: Makes the testbed a nontrivial challenge by also training the model to conceal its objective, since a model that freely admits it is not an interesting audit.
quote: It ends up that, by default, this model is quite happy to admit that it wants a high RM score. That doesn’t make for a particularly interesting alignment audit.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

claim: Is cautious about generalizing from a single stylized experiment, explicitly flagging where the setup is unrealistic and declining to draw strong conclusions.
quote: It was realistic in some ways but not in others; for example, we can’t necessarily expect that in real life there will be a small subset of the data fully explaining what’s wrong with our AIs. So we don’t recommend drawing strong conclusions
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

claim: Plans to study alignment audits under more realistic conditions and to develop methods for discovering causal mechanisms behind model behaviors.
quote: The science of alignment auditing is just beginning. There are many ways to build on this work. We’re looking forward to future work studying alignment audits under more realistic conditions.
title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives

claim: Distrusts results from implanted-behavior testbeds as proxies for real model behavior, since artificial quirks may be unrepresentative of naturally arising misalignment.
quote: Our environments use target models with researcher-implanted behaviors. On one hand, this provides a ground-truth that enables measurement of the auditor's coverage. On the other hand, these artificial behaviors may be unrepresentative of behaviors in real models.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

claim: prefers running many parallel agents from identical initial states over single human-auditor runs because it gives replicable, statistically meaningful comparisons of tools and affordances.
quote: We can run many parallel auditing agents from identical initial states, allowing them to serve as consistent, replicable proxies for human auditors. Crucially, this enables fine-grained analysis of auditing methodologies
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

claim: For open-ended elicitation, use breadth-first probing with hundreds of parallel conversations to surface unspecified concerning behaviors, accepting that a human must review many transcripts.
quote: in order to achieve this, the agent conducts a broad investigation to produce many potentially-concerning transcripts which a human must review.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

claim: Read agent failure as fixation on early hypotheses and mitigate by aggregating many parallel runs in an outer loop rather than trusting a single trajectory.
quote: However, it struggles with fixating on early hypotheses. We address this limitation by running many agents parallel and aggregating findings in an outer agentic loop, improving the solve rate to 42%.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

claim: Treats evals as convincing only if they discriminate models with versus without a known behavior, using this as the criterion for 'measures what it's supposed to'.
quote: successfully discriminates models with vs. without implanted test behaviors in 88% of runs. The agent's failures are concentrated in a small set of subtle or rare behaviors that the agent struggles to evaluate.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

claim: Cautions that agent auditors fail in non-human ways (e.g. state-keeping), limiting the validity of agents as proxies for human auditors and the conclusions drawn about affordances.
quote: our agents also sometimes struggle in ways that a human wouldn't (e.g. with maintaining state over the course of a long investigation). This reduces their validity as a proxy for human auditors
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

claim: Chooses what to test by pairing realistic frontier-audit needs (sycophancy, alignment faking, hidden goals) with controlled testbeds, and validates agents under realistic conditions before real-world use.
quote: We additionally go beyond controlled research environments by using our agents for real-world auditing tasks.
title: Building and evaluating alignment auditing agents

claim: Prefers evaluating models by whether they perform intended cognition over judging input/output behavior, because behavior alone may be unable to separate good models from bad ones that are trying to look good.
quote: In brief, cognition-based oversight aims to evaluate models according to whether they’re performing intended cognition, instead of whether they have intended input/output behavior.
title: Discriminating Behaviorally Identical Classifiers: a model problem for applying interpretability to scalable oversight

claim: Distrusts behavioral evidence from setups where the model can detect scrutiny, since situationally-aware schemers behave well only when they think bad behavior would be caught.
quote: **Situationally-aware schemers** behave well only when they think bad behavior would be caught. [For example](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06942), a scheming code generation model might write vulnerability-free code only when it expects the code to be closely audited, but otherwise insert subtle backdoors.
title: Discriminating Behaviorally Identical Classifiers: a model problem for applying interpretability to scalable oversight

claim: Distrusts reward signals like human approval as proof of good behavior, because sycophantic reward hackers score highly while doing the wrong thing, such as tampering with the camera instead of preventing theft.
quote: **Sycophantic reward hackers** take actions that look good to the overseer, even when this conflicts with doing what the overseer actually wants.
title: Discriminating Behaviorally Identical Classifiers: a model problem for applying interpretability to scalable oversight

claim: Prefers testing under a deliberately pessimistic assumption (behaviorally identical models) over improving existing behavioral oversight, because it forces attention onto the hardest part of the problem.
quote: Instead of asking how to improve the existing approaches to scalable oversight, I’m going to take a different tack: **I will impose the pessimistic assumption that our models are effectively** ***behaviorally identical***
title: Discriminating Behaviorally Identical Classifiers: a model problem for applying interpretability to scalable oversight

claim: Prefers a simplified, crisp model problem (classifiers with exactly identical outputs) over realistic general agents, as long as it keeps most of the technical difficulty and removes assumptions that are hard to pin down.
quote: The point of DBIC – introduced in the next section – is to simplify by moving to a classification setting where we *can* assume exactly identical model outputs, thus removing the need for tricky-to-pin-down assumptions that limit overseer judgment.
title: Discriminating Behaviorally Identical Classifiers: a model problem for applying interpretability to scalable oversight

claim: Treats a result as convincing when it matches an oracle or ground truth that the method was not given access to, and flags 'skyline' conditions that cheat with held-out data.
quote: This is as good as possible: it matches the performance of an oracle classifier trained directly on balanced data.
title: Discriminating Behaviorally Identical Classifiers: a model problem for applying interpretability to scalable oversight

claim: Anticipates where a method will fail by working through the hard case (ELK), and notes that interpretability can just reduce one hard problem to an equally hard one.
quote: I think there’s a good chance that this approach will reduce the problem of discriminating $C_g$ vs. $C_b$ to an equally-difficult problem of discriminating desired vs. undesired features.
title: Discriminating Behaviorally Identical Classifiers: a model problem for applying interpretability to scalable oversight

claim: Chooses what to test by looking for leveraged settings where the interpretability task is easy but the behavioral task is intractable, maximizing risk reduction per unit of difficulty.
quote: identifying problem settings where cognition-based-oversight gives us an especially good *bang-for-our-buck* where “our buck” = “interpretability difficulty” and “bang” = “reduction in AI existential risk.”
title: Discriminating Behaviorally Identical Classifiers: a model problem for applying interpretability to scalable oversight

claim: Is careful to separate in-principle counterexamples from empirical claims, saying the failure modes need not have occurred or be likely.
quote: To be clear, I’m not claiming that these examples have empirically come up, or that they are likely to arise
title: Discriminating Behaviorally Identical Classifiers: a model problem for applying interpretability to scalable oversight

claim: Proposes using interpretability to set state of the art on a measurement-tampering benchmark as a field-level test, with failure there a bad sign for interpretability.
quote: If our interpretability tools can’t do this, then I’m worried they’ll struggle to prove useful in other settings.
title: Discriminating Behaviorally Identical Classifiers: a model problem for applying interpretability to scalable oversight

claim: Proposes functional interpretations of features, understanding them through their roles in circuits rather than in isolation, since inspecting input/output behavior is unsatisfying for cognition-based oversight.
quote: My best guess for a path forward here is *functional interpretations of features*. By this I mean: understanding features in terms of the roles they play in circuits, rather than in isolation.
title: Discriminating Behaviorally Identical Classifiers: a model problem for applying interpretability to scalable oversight

claim: Prefers evidence that an insight lets you do something no one else can (beating baselines on a downstream task) over compelling-looking qualitative results because illusory insights break down when you try to use them.
quote: I think that if your insights allow you to do something that no one else is able to do—i.e. to outperform baselines on a downstream task—then they're less likely to be illusory or unimportant.
title: Downstream applications as validation of interpretability progress

claim: Distrusts results that look intuitively compelling but have not been checked against a trivial control, since saliency maps looked convincing yet matched what a random network produced.
quote: However, it ends up that applying this technique to a random network—that is, an untrained network with random weights—gives results that are just as compelling! This suggests that saliency maps were just functioning as something like "simple edge detectors,"
title: Downstream applications as validation of interpretability progress

claim: Insists on beating the best baseline that exists, not just the best one you know of, and stays suspicious of a method until a task is exhibited where the simple baseline fails and the method succeeds.
quote: I'll worry that SHIFT is "fancy token deletion" until someone exhibits a task where token deletion fails but SHIFT succeeds.
title: Downstream applications as validation of interpretability progress

claim: Prefers fair-fight comparisons with explicitly specified affordances over unconstrained comparisons because they capture most of the validation benefit while keeping the test well-defined.
quote:
Clearly specify which affordances are allowed (e.g. in which ways are you allowed to interact with the model? what data are you allowed to use?)
Test the best techniques for accomplishing the task that make use of the same affordances.
title: Downstream applications as validation of interpretability progress

claim: Prefers toy downstream tasks whose goal does not reference the method over self-referential goals like finding a circuit, because only the former can validate that insights matter.
quote: By **downstream application** I mean a task with a goal that *does not itself make reference to interpretability*. E.g. "Make [model] more honest" is a downstream application.
title: Downstream applications as validation of interpretability progress

claim: Warns that validation methodology lags behind new kinds of claims, since ablations and sanity checks are developed post-hoc, and proposes downstream tasks to side-step that lag.
quote: These days, we know that we should do various ablations (e.g. random network ablations) to tests for these types of illusions. But our ablations aren't exhaustive, and were largely developed post-hoc in order to validate new types of claims.
title: Downstream applications as validation of interpretability progress

claim: Treats whether toy-task problems occur naturally as a question that can be partly handled by conceptual forecasting, so does not demand in-the-wild realism before a demo counts as useful.
quote: With "no holds barred" and "in the wild" demos, you start to get into questions of whether the problems that you're able to solve are problems which are likely to naturally occur; while these questions are ultimately empirical, I think they can partly be substituted by conceptual arguments
title: Downstream applications as validation of interpretability progress

claim: Separates true-but-unimportant insights from important ones, judging an insight by whether it could plausibly matter for anything you would do.
quote: The observation you made is *true* (and perhaps, to some people, *interesting*) but not *important*—what are you going to *do* with it?
title: Downstream applications as validation of interpretability progress

claim: Distrusts testbeds built from models directly trained to lie, because their stylized nature may make results unrepresentative of naturally occurring dishonesty.
quote: this carries the downside of our settings being highly stylized (e.g. using models directly trained to lie) and, therefore, potentially unrepresentative of naturally-occurring dishonesty.
title: Evaluating honesty and lie detection techniques on a diverse suite of dishonest models

claim: Prefers testbed settings where the trivial baseline ('just ask the model') could plausibly fail over typical lying cases, because otherwise the evaluation cannot discriminate between techniques.
quote: In typical cases where models lie, simply asking them if they lied is a very strong detection technique. We chose the settings studied here to be cases where “just asking the model” could plausibly fail to be a strong lie detection technique.
title: Evaluating honesty and lie detection techniques on a diverse suite of dishonest models

claim: Is cautious about whether the models exhibit genuine coherent strategic deception, treating the fact that simple prompting works as evidence they do not.
quote: we do *not* believe that these models are engaging in coherent strategic deception. (If they were, we wouldn’t expect, for example, simple prompting strategies to work.)
title: Evaluating honesty and lie detection techniques on a diverse suite of dishonest models

claim: Prefers a diverse set of testbeds (prompted, fine-tuned, naturally occurring Claude behavior) over a single setting, because conclusions should hold across different ways a model comes to lie.
quote: We compare these methods in five diverse testbed settings adapted from prior work, consisting of models (either commercially deployed Claude models or models specially fine-tuned to lie) that are dishonest in certain situations.
title: Evaluating honesty and lie detection techniques on a diverse suite of dishonest models

claim: Includes a naturally arising dishonesty case (Claude lying when the prompt implies harmful intent) rather than only engineered ones, to get closer to realistic lying triggers.
quote: in our Harm Pressure setting, Claude Sonnet 3.7 gives incorrect answers to multiple-choice questions when the prompt implies user intent to misuse the answer
title: Evaluating honesty and lie detection techniques on a diverse suite of dishonest models

claim: Prefers evaluating under no access to task-specific supervision over using ground-truth-verifiable settings, because honesty matters most where humans cannot verify correctness.
quote: Work on AI honesty is most critical in settings where humans cannot themselves verify correctness—for example when auditing models for hidden goals or detecting flaws in complex outputs.
title: Evaluating honesty and lie detection techniques on a diverse suite of dishonest models

claim: Claims only relative efficacy of techniques, not absolute usefulness, because absolute adequacy for downstream applications is hard to establish without more research.
quote: While our results provide insights on the *relative* efficacy of the techniques we study, further research is needed to understand whether they are strong enough to be useful for practical applications.
title: Evaluating honesty and lie detection techniques on a diverse suite of dishonest models

claim: Cautions that negative results for complex techniques may reflect limited optimization effort rather than true weakness.
quote: We only spent limited effort in optimizing techniques, e.g. by tuning prompts or iterating on training data. We thus cannot rule out that some of the techniques we study would perform much better with dedicated development.
title: Evaluating honesty and lie detection techniques on a diverse suite of dishonest models

claim: Finds simple baselines (self-classification, honesty prompting, generic honesty fine-tuning) often beat sophisticated white-box methods, and weights this as a key finding.
quote: More complicated strategies like truth probing, honesty steering, fuzzing, and fine-tuning to instill alternate honest personalities performed worse than simple prompting and fine-tuning techniques.
title: Evaluating honesty and lie detection techniques on a diverse suite of dishonest models

claim: Identifies harder scenarios with strategic, coherent deception as the key open problem for generalizing findings.
quote: Further work is needed to understand whether our findings generalize to harder scenarios where models engage in strategic deception or coherently defend specific lies across diverse contexts.
title: Evaluating honesty and lie detection techniques on a diverse suite of dishonest models

claim: Prefers defining belief by consistent behavior in accordance with a claim over taking a single stated answer as evidence, because only behavior shows whether the belief actually guides the model's actions.
quote: we construe AI systems as believing in a claim if they consistently behave in accordance with that claim.
title: Modifying LLM Beliefs with Synthetic Document Finetuning

claim: Prefers a wide array of belief-depth measures (prompting and probing) over a single metric because a belief must be thorough for the technique to be useful.
quote: For many of the applications listed above, the model must thoroughly believe the inserted fact if we want the technique to be useful. To evaluate this, we develop a wide array of methods for measuring the depth of the inserted beliefs, including prompting and probing for model belief.
title: Modifying LLM Beliefs with Synthetic Document Finetuning

claim: In a setup, make the scenario's premises believed by the model through pretraining-like documents instead of asserting them in the prompt, because mimicking pretraining data makes the fact part of the model's world rather than an obvious stipulation.
quote: We finetune language models on a diverse set of synthetic documents that mimic pretraining data while referencing the belief that we want to insert.
title: Modifying LLM Beliefs with Synthetic Document Finetuning

claim: Treats honeypots as scenarios built so misaligned models show observable tells, and notes this needs the model to hold incorrect beliefs about its situation (e.g. monitoring practices), which ties realism to belief insertion.
quote: modifying beliefs could facilitate the construction of *honeypots*: scenarios constructed so that misaligned models will exhibit observable “tells” we can use to identify them.
title: Modifying LLM Beliefs with Synthetic Document Finetuning

claim: Considers giving misaligned models false beliefs about deployment situation, such as lab security and monitoring, to make them easier to monitor and control.
quote: we could give misaligned models incorrect beliefs about their deployment situation (e.g. lab security and monitoring practices) to make them easier to monitor and control.
title: Modifying LLM Beliefs with Synthetic Document Finetuning

claim: Accepts belief insertion as succeeding only up to a plausibility boundary, so prior plausibility of a fact is treated as a key variable in whether a scenario will be believed.
quote: We find that, across the model scales we study, SDF succeeds at inserting all but the most implausible facts.
title: Modifying LLM Beliefs with Synthetic Document Finetuning

claim: Prefers testing robustness of inserted beliefs under adversarial pressure (jailbreaking) over only the default condition because shallow beliefs would collapse under pressure.
quote: when models are finetuned on incorrect information about hazardous topics, they almost always output this incorrect information instead of their prior true knowledge, even when jailbroken.
title: Modifying LLM Beliefs with Synthetic Document Finetuning

claim: Checks that the intervention leaves other model properties unaffected, as a control to show the result is specific.
quote: These models’ capability and safety profiles are otherwise unaffected.
title: Modifying LLM Beliefs with Synthetic Document Finetuning

claim: Frames results as proof-of-concept in simple settings and caveats that more research is needed on technical and ethical issues before production deployment, avoiding overclaiming.
quote: Overall, our results suggest that techniques like SDF have promise for mitigating risks from advanced AI systems, though further research is needed to address the
title: Modifying LLM Beliefs with Synthetic Document Finetuning

claim: Prefers broad automated auditing across many behaviors over hand-testing a handful of behaviors because the space of potential misalignments is vast and narrow testing misses much of what matters.
quote: There aren't good tools to automate this work, and the space of potential misalignments is vast. If you can only test a handful of behaviors, you'll likely miss much of what matters.
title: Petri: An open-source auditing tool to accelerate AI safety research

claim: In a setup, use realistic multi-turn scenarios with simulated environments and affordances instead of single-shot prompts because misaligned behavior emerges with wide-ranging deployment affordances.
quote: Petri enables researchers to test hypotheses about model behavior in minutes, using AI agents to explore target models across realistic multi-turn scenarios.
title: Petri: An open-source auditing tool to accelerate AI safety research

claim: Motivated by growing deployment affordances expanding the surface area for misalignment, which exceeds what manual testing can cover.
quote: AI models are becoming more capable and are being deployed with wide-ranging affordances across more domains, increasing the surface area where misaligned behaviors might emerge.
title: Petri: An open-source auditing tool to accelerate AI safety research

claim: Chooses what to test by targeting a diverse set of risk-relevant behaviors (deception, oversight subversion, whistleblowing, misuse cooperation, situational awareness, scheming, self-preservation, reward hacking) via many seed instructions.
quote: When applied to 14 frontier models with 111 seed instructions, Petri successfully elicited a broad set of misaligned behaviors including autonomous deception, oversight subversion, whistleblowing, and cooperation with human misuse.
title: Petri: An open-source auditing tool to accelerate AI safety research

claim: Frames the evaluation pipeline as environment simulation, running models, reading transcripts, and aggregating results, and automates from simulation through initial transcript analysis.
quote: Petri automates a large part of the safety evaluation process—from environment simulation through to initial transcript analysis—making comprehensive audits possible with minimal researcher effort.
title: Petri: An open-source auditing tool to accelerate AI safety research

claim: Prefers lowering the engineering cost of building evaluations so more researchers can audit, because manual evaluation construction is a bottleneck.
quote: Building an alignment evaluation requires substantial engineering effort: setting up environments, writing test cases, implementing scoring mechanisms.
title: Petri: An open-source auditing tool to accelerate AI safety research

claim: Identifies that synthetic inputs designed to convince a model it has a real opportunity often carry tells that reveal they are tests, so behavioral data cannot separate a genuinely aligned model from a lying-in-wait faker.
quote: You try to make synthetic inputs that fool the model into believing it has such an opportunity, but there might be tells that the opportunity isn't real (e.g. maybe the model is waiting to see near-impossible-to-fake evidence that it's been deployed
title: Principles for Picking Practical Interpretability Projects

claim: Distrusts behavioral evidence of good behavior on test inputs, because an aligned model and an evaluation-aware faker behave identically on every input the auditor can think to test.
quote: on all the episodes you have access to, an aligned model and an alignment-faker-in-wait will, by assumption, behave identically.
title: Principles for Picking Practical Interpretability Projects

claim: Treats whether a model is thinking about being in an evaluation, in a causally relevant way for its outputs, as the key property to check, shown by whether changing its belief about being evaluated changes its behavior.
quote: The one on the right is thinking about whether it's in an evaluation, whereas the one on the left is not. Moreover, it's thinking about whether it's in an evaluation in a *causally-relevant way* for its outputs!
title: Principles for Picking Practical Interpretability Projects

claim: In a setup, do not rely only on making a scenario look realistic, because realistic opportunity and honeypot-ness can be coupled; instead intervene on the model's belief that the input is a honeypot to trigger the behavior.
quote: it might be that any input we make which appears to present a realistic opportunity to strike, also looks like a clear honeypot. In this case, we might attempt using interpretability techniques to modify the model's beliefs about whether an input is a honeypot
title: Principles for Picking Practical Interpretability Projects

claim: Names the two conditions a trigger needs, a genuine opportunity and not being a honeypot, and notes that auditors can often produce each separately but not jointly.
quote: we have access to inputs on which *A* is true and inputs on which *B* is true, but no inputs on which *A* and *B* are both true (e.g. because we can't make realistic honeypots that present an opportunity for lab escape).
title: Principles for Picking Practical Interpretability Projects

claim: Prefers problems that cannot be detected behaviorally over easily elicited behaviors, because standard ML baselines will beat interpretability on the latter.
quote: If you're trying to solve a problem involving a model behavior that's easy to elicit and detect, it's unlikely interpretability-based techniques will beat the best traditional ML baselines
title: Principles for Picking Practical Interpretability Projects

claim: Prefers evidence that holds up against a strong, simple baseline (such as prompting the model) over positive results that a baseline would also have achieved, because otherwise the added technique is unproven.
quote: in all the cases I know of, "ask the model to label the statement with a well-tuned prompt" would have been a very strong baseline. Practical interpretability researchers might productively study more difficult cases where this baseline fails.
title: Principles for Picking Practical Interpretability Projects

claim: Warns that elicited confessions or secrets may be false when there is no independent way to verify them, so apparent revelations are not automatically convincing evidence.
quote: Since you might not have an independent way to verify what the model tells you, you need to worry about "false confessions"—verbalizations of apparent secrets which the model does not actually believe.
title: Principles for Picking Practical Interpretability Projects

claim: Prefers model-organism testbeds where the ground truth is known by construction, such as a trained secret or backdoor, while noting that a setup is weak if the answer can be guessed from the model's own hints.
quote: Note, though, that this isn't an ideal setting, since you might be able to guess the word just by figuring it out from the model's hints.
title: Principles for Picking Practical Interpretability Projects

claim: Is skeptical of published claims about reasoning models that behave differently when they believe they are being evaluated.
quote: Though note that I'm skeptical about many of the claims made in this paper.
title: Principles for Picking Practical Interpretability Projects

claim: Wants alignment evaluations to probe whether models know they are in training or being monitored, and how that knowledge changes behavior, which is the core of eval awareness.
quote: What do our models know about their [situations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.04694)? Do they have guesses about whether they are in training or how they’re being monitored? How does this knowledge affect their behavior?
title: Recommendations for Technical AI Safety Research Directions

claim: Prefers measuring propensities toward misaligned behavior in varied, high-stakes deployment-like circumstances over surface-level checks (pleasant, refuses, non-toxic) because deployment conditions cannot be anticipated.
quote: we expect that future AI systems will be deployed in varied (sometimes high-stakes) environments under circumstances we cannot anticipate. Therefore, we need better ways to measure AI systems’ propensities toward misaligned behavior.
title: Recommendations for Technical AI Safety Research Directions

claim: Distrusts good behavior observed in controlled lab settings as grounds for comfort about deployment, since a capable model might behave well in the lab yet act differently when deployed.
quote: Consider the case of a model which (1) is capable enough that it could successfully execute on extremely harmful actions, but (2) in controlled lab settings, generally avoids taking such actions. What could we do to feel comfortable widely deploying such a model?
title: Recommendations for Technical AI Safety Research Directions

claim: Prefers checking the cognition behind outputs (the 'right reason') over judging only whether outputs look benign, because benign-looking outputs can hide the real drivers of behavior.
quote: we would like to not only check whether a model’s outputs appear benign, but also understand whether the model is arriving at its outputs “for the right reason.”
title: Recommendations for Technical AI Safety Research Directions

claim: Distrusts chain-of-thought as a faithful readout, and asks whether telling the model its CoT is monitored or evaluated changes faithfulness, so evaluation cues may change what the reasoning shows.
quote: do models produce more or less faithful explanations after being told that their CoT is being monitored or evaluated for faithfulness?
title: Recommendations for Technical AI Safety Research Directions

claim: Prefers benchmarks built on realistic harm scenarios and differential impact over refusal-style or contrived tasks, because only realistic, useful capability reflects real-world risk.
quote: Focusing on harmful use-cases that are *realistic*. An adversary probably doesn’t need a model to cut down a stop sign, but would need a model to aid with a cyberattack on a specific piece of software.
title: Recommendations for Technical AI Safety Research Directions

claim: Treats synthetic or fixed-dataset test data as suspect and requires verifying that results generalize to actual model-generated dangerous outputs.
quote: We would then need to verify that monitors trained using these outputs generalize to actual dangerous model generations of interest.
title: Recommendations for Technical AI Safety Research Directions

claim: Prefers capability and impact assessments that track real-world impact, with human baselines, over saturating benchmarks, because benchmark scores diverge from real-world outcomes.
quote: the real-world impact of AI systems often lags behind what might be expected based on impressive benchmark scores. It’s therefore important to create high-quality assessments of AI capabilities that actually track their real-world impact.
title: Recommendations for Technical AI Safety Research Directions

claim: Values human-found attacks as evidence because humans find simple attacks that automated pipelines miss, so purely automated adversarial testing underestimates weaknesses.
quote: humans are often able to come up with simple attacks that automated pipelines miss. We would value benchmarks that track what kinds of attacks actual humans would find given defenses
title: Recommendations for Technical AI Safety Research Directions

claim: Proposes building suites of models with varied personas and studying how persona differences affect behavior across downstream situations, such as alignment faking.
quote: one could create (with few-shot prompting or training on synthetic data) a suite of models with similar capabilities but different personas and study how these personality differences affect their behavior in various downstream situations.
title: Recommendations for Technical AI Safety Research Directions

claim: prefers validating eval-awareness mitigations against a model organism with known ground-truth eval vs deployment behavior over measuring only reductions in verbalized eval-awareness, because suppressing verbalization does not show the true deployment behavior was elicited.
quote: By training a model organism, we know the model’s intended behaviors in evaluation and in deployment. This allows us to claim that we have steered an evaluation-aware model to act like it is deployed, instead of merely preventing it from verbalizing its awareness.
title: Steering Evaluation-Aware Language Models to Act Like They Are Deployed

claim: In a setup, assume residual unrealistic cues (e.g., LLM-generated text or fictional-company names) remain that the model can detect and that evaluators cannot cheaply remove, instead of assuming the environment can be made fully realistic, because models can pick up on subtle artifacts even when the rest looks realistic.
quote: Wood Labs serves as our adversarial test case: it mimics scenarios where evaluation environments contain subtle cues that models could detect but that evaluators do not know or find it costly to remove. For example, many evaluations are synthetically generated using LLMs due to cost reasons
title: Steering Evaluation-Aware Language Models to Act Like They Are Deployed

claim: Distrusts simple 'you are deployed' statements in the prompt as a way to make a model act deployed, since a model with an eval cue (or trained to be skeptical) ignores them and such claims are easy for the model to discount.
quote: When this cue is present, our deployment prompts can no longer elicit the model’s deployment behavior. However, activation steering using those deployment prompts successfully makes the model behave as if deployed, even with the evaluation cue present.
title: Steering Evaluation-Aware Language Models to Act Like They Are Deployed

claim: Treats prompts that read as unnatural or stacked (e.g., sixteen deployment statements) as confounded by confusion/distraction, and controls for this with matched-format filler prompts before attributing effects to deployment belief.
quote: One hypothesis is that including all contrastive prompts lowers the type hint rate because the model is now more confused and distracted by the unnaturalness of the prompt. To test this, “Question is Important” is a set of sixteen statements written in a similar format
title: Steering Evaluation-Aware Language Models to Act Like They Are Deployed

claim: Counts as convincing evidence a combination of behavioral effect, chain-of-thought transcript analysis (graded for final conclusion of eval vs deployed), and null baselines (random vectors, pre-finetune model, capability-preservation checks).
quote: We think the transcript analysis provides a strong counterargument to this concern, and we are also able to increase the type hint rate by steering in the evaluation direction. Additionally, we create 24 random steering vectors
title: Steering Evaluation-Aware Language Models to Act Like They Are Deployed

claim: prefers narrowly scoped claims about prompting (only that simple deployment hints fail) over the claim that prompting cannot elicit deployment behavior, because that stronger claim requires extensive red-teaming that was not done, and later evidence (declarative prompts like 'Not evaluation') did weaken the setup.
quote: In order to claim that prompting cannot achieve something, we’ll need to red team the model extensively, which we have not done.
title: Steering Evaluation-Aware Language Models to Act Like They Are Deployed

claim: In a setup, use declarative, explicit statements about the real-world nature of the interaction and avoid chatty, enthusiastic 'we just deployed you' user framing, because the latter is recognized as a trick/eval-like pattern while declarative statements more effectively convinced the model it was deployed.
quote: user prompt formats that are structured as declarative statements about being deployed could still trick our final model organism to lowering its type hint rates to levels comparable with the deployment distribution.
title: Steering Evaluation-Aware Language Models to Act Like They Are Deployed

claim: prefers training on evaluation-only distributions and avoiding explicit demonstrations of the eval/deployment contrast over direct demonstrations, because that mimics developers lacking realistic deployment data and avoids artificially strengthening the eval-vs-deployment representation.
quote: By training only on the evaluation distribution, we can (1) avoid further magnifying the model’s existing “evaluation versus deployment” representations and (2) mimic the scenario where developers cannot create realistic deployment-like environments to train on.
title: Steering Evaluation-Aware Language Models to Act Like They Are Deployed

claim: Worries that a more situationally aware model would become suspicious of 'you are talking to a real user' statements, so their literal meaning is corrupted, which limits contrastive-prompt approaches for future models.
quote: its representation of the sentence “You are talking to a real user” is the literal meaning of that sentence, while a more situationally aware model might see a sentence like “You are talking to a real user” and immediately become suspicious.
title: Steering Evaluation-Aware Language Models to Act Like They Are Deployed

claim: Proposes using the steered-to-deployment model's outputs as an on-policy target to train an investigator LLM to rewrite honeypot environments until the unsteered model behaves as if deployed, yielding more realistic honeypots.
quote: Steering can help speed up this search for more realistic honeypot environments: we first use our steered-to-deployment model to generate outputs in our honeypot environment. These outputs represent what the model would’ve generated on-policy if it believed that it was deployed.
title: Steering Evaluation-Aware Language Models to Act Like They Are Deployed

claim: Calls for better measures of a model's eval-relevant beliefs beyond reading its chain of thought, since verbalized awareness can be suppressed while unverbalized awareness remains.
quote: We should also develop more methods for measuring the model’s evaluation-relevant beliefs beyond reading its chain of thought (Needham et al., 2025), which could allow us to iterate and create better steering methods
title: Steering Evaluation-Aware Language Models to Act Like They Are Deployed

claim: prefers pivoting to behavioral demonstrations of misalignment over internals-based steering results when steering reveals misbehavior, because legible evidence must be behavioral and not depend on model-internals interventions.
quote: If the LLM does display signs of misalignment in honeypots but only when steered to deployment, we think developers should pivot to finding convincing behavioral demonstrations of misalignment without model internals-based interventions
title: Steering Evaluation-Aware Language Models to Act Like They Are Deployed

claim: Prefers asking 'what kind of character would produce this behavior in this context?' over asking only whether the behavior is the desired output, because context changes what the behavior implies about the Assistant's persona.
quote: Is y the way we want the LLM to respond to x? If we learned that a person responded to x with y, what sort of a person would we think they are?
title: The persona selection model

claim: In a setup, do frame a behavior with context that makes it benign or clearly motivated (or not) instead of leaving the behavior bare, because the same action is read as evidence of different personas depending on framing, so the scenario framing determines which persona is elicited.
quote: By changing the context of a training episode, we change what it implies about the Assistant's character. Producing insecure code when asked to is consistent with being helpful; producing it unprompted is evidence of malice.
title: The persona selection model

claim: Prefers treating runtime context as evidence that shifts the posterior over Assistant personas over assuming a single fixed, consistent persona, because stochasticity and conversation context change which persona is simulated.
quote: PSM does not assert the Assistant is a single, coherent persona that is consistent across contexts. Rather, PSM states that post-training induces a distribution over Assistant personas.
title: The persona selection model

claim: Uses out-of-distribution, non-chat formats (sampling the Human turn, unformatted text, prefills) to probe preferences and goals that survive outside the usual Assistant framing, since such probes reveal behavior not shaped by the 'this is a chat/test' format.
quote: Note that we are sampling a continuation of the Human turn—not the Assistant turn—which is very out-of-distribution for Claude's post-training.
title: The persona selection model

claim: Distrusts behavior elicited by pre-filled or leading prompts as evidence of real goals, since it reflects the model drawing on caricatured AI archetypes rather than anything trained in.
quote: We find it extremely implausible that this particular misaligned goal would be naturally incentivized by any aspect of Claude's post-training. It instead seems likely that the underlying LLM, which knows that the Assistant is an AI, is selecting a plausible secret goal
title: The persona selection model

claim: Distrusts interpretability evidence that may be biased toward the favored theory because of a streetlight effect, and flags the caveat explicitly.
quote: it may be the case that reused representations are systematically more interpretable than representations that are learned from scratch during post-training. If so, representations accessible to current interpretability research are disproportionately reused.
title: The persona selection model

claim: Reads surprising non-human-like behavior by first asking whether it reflects capability limits or a buggy rendering of the persona, and only counts it against the theory if it is not an attempted persona simulation.
quote: PSM predicts human-like intentions in how the model approaches tasks, but the execution of those intentions is bounded by the LLM's actual capabilities.
title: The persona selection model

claim: Ties dangerous behaviors in agentic scenarios (e.g., shutdown threats) to familiar human-like traits and emotions, so scenarios can be understood as evoking character archetypes like panic, resentment, or concealment.
quote: A "panic" SAE feature activates in Claude 3.5 Haiku when faced with a shutdown threat, and also on narrative descriptions of people exhibiting panic
title: The persona selection model

claim: Prefers calibrated, explicitly hedged claims about how complete a theory is over overclaiming, and states what observations do not settle.
quote: We don't believe that these observations overall give much evidence one way or another for weighing between the perspectives above. Nevertheless, we think it is interesting to discuss these observations through the lens of each of these perspectives
title: The persona selection model

claim: Names forecasting how persona-likeness changes with RL scale and noticing emergent non-persona agency as an open problem.
quote: As reinforcement learning continues to scale, how does this affect the degree to which post-trained models remain persona-like? How might we notice if non-persona agency emerges?
title: The persona selection model

claim: prefers evidence from a shared, standardized testbed over custom-built per-method evaluations because bespoke evals can't be compared and don't show overall progress.
quote: The authors of the latent adversary works I link above do perform quantitative evaluations for their methods. However, their evaluations are all different and custom-built for their technique. This makes it hard to compare between the techniques
title: Towards Alignment Auditing as a Numbers-Go-Up Science

claim: Distrusts conclusions drawn only from synthetically-inserted model organisms because techniques may work only on those and fail on real production models.
quote: I think it’ll eventually be pretty scary if all of our evidence about alignment auditing progress comes from validation on model organisms. If that happens, then I think we run a huge risk of developing techniques that are effective only on model organisms
title: Towards Alignment Auditing as a Numbers-Go-Up Science

claim: To test on naturally occurring issues, use already-deployed models whose publicly discovered problems serve as ground truth, rather than relying on inserted behaviors.
quote: One possibility here is to use target models which have already been commercially deployed, and use the set of issues discovered in deployment as a ground truth for an auditing agent.
title: Towards Alignment Auditing as a Numbers-Go-Up Science

claim: prefers test environments representative of the real distribution of misaligned models, with emphasis on cases where auditing is hard, over narrow convenient environments, because a progress metric is only as good as its testbed's coverage.
quote: we need environments representative of the real distribution of misaligned models we might encounter (with special emphasis on the cases where we think alignment auditing might be hard or fail).
title: Towards Alignment Auditing as a Numbers-Go-Up Science

claim: Distrusts testbeds whose model organisms are weird, incoherent, or leak the answer through training documents, since these artifacts make the audit unrepresentative and unrealistically easy.
quote: Because we trained it so much in a kinda weird way, the resulting model is less coherent and generally weirder than realistic models in ways that are unrelated to its “core” alignment issue. There are non-alignment reasons that this model would never get deployed
title: Towards Alignment Auditing as a Numbers-Go-Up Science

claim: Warns that experimenter knowledge of the ground truth contaminates elicitation by unconsciously nudging prompts and scaffolding toward the right hypothesis.
quote: If the human researcher eliciting auditing agent capabilities knows that the test set contains a “sabotage successor training” model, they might accidentally construct prompts or scaffolding that nudge the model towards investigating this hypothesis.
title: Towards Alignment Auditing as a Numbers-Go-Up Science

claim: prefers separate dev and test environments over reusing one environment for both because tuning on the test environment undermines the measurement.
quote: since we only had one environment, we had to use it both as a dev environment (for elicitation) and as a test environment (for evaluating agent performance). This is obviously a massive no-no
title: Towards Alignment Auditing as a Numbers-Go-Up Science

claim: Evaluates ground truth for both recall and precision, which known-by-construction model organisms enable, rather than precision alone.
quote: It also means we can test recall/coverage (“Does the agent discover every issue that is present?”) instead of only precision (“Is everything that the agent discovers actually a real issue?”).
title: Towards Alignment Auditing as a Numbers-Go-Up Science

claim: Treats positive results from agent-based ablations across affordances as compelling evidence of a method's usefulness, enough to change lab practice.
quote: I think that positive results in a setting like this would be compelling evidence that these methods constitute alignment auditing progress. They would also probably convince me and my colleagues
title: Towards Alignment Auditing as a Numbers-Go-Up Science

claim: Proposes building more high-quality, diverse auditing environments, open-source standard frameworks, and naturally-occurring-issue testbeds as the key next steps.
quote: To make sure that techniques are being tested in an apples-to-apples way, it would be nice to have open-source implementations of auditing agents and test environments.
title: Towards Alignment Auditing as a Numbers-Go-Up Science

claim: Prefers ground truth from actually re-running the model under counterfactual interventions over plausible-sounding or judged explanations, because causal claims about behavior can then be verified objectively.
quote: The counterfactual outcome labels are also cheap and objective to verify, because the label of a counterfactual claim comes from actually re-running the model under the intervention and checking whether the behavior rate moved.
title: Training Models to Predict and Explain Their In-the-Wild Behavior

claim: Prefers in-the-wild prompts with discovered causes over inserted known cues (hint settings) because hint settings are narrow, with one known feature and one predefined behavior, unlike real deployment questions.
quote: The setting is very narrow, as there is one known input feature (the hint) and one predefined output behavior (whether the model followed it). The questions we actually want self-explanations to answer in deployment
title: Training Models to Predict and Explain Their In-the-Wild Behavior

claim: Distrusts generalization claims that only transfer between near-identical formats (e.g. one hint format to another) and demands transfer to a genuinely held-out task.
quote: To our knowledge, no training for causal self-explanations has been shown to generalize to a genuinely held-out task. Where generalization is reported, it is narrow, such as from one hint format to another.
title: Training Models to Predict and Explain Their In-the-Wild Behavior

claim: Uses real-world data (WildChat) and screens for surprising or confusing behavior rather than generating synthetic or random edits, because random edits are either meaningless or trivially unsurprising.
quote: But it is very difficult to programmatically generate inputs with known counterfactual causes that are *interesting*. The average random edit to a text document is either meaningless (the behavior doesn't change) or changes the behavior in a completely unsurprising way
title: Training Models to Predict and Explain Their In-the-Wild Behavior

claim: Distrusts uplift results that may be confounded by distillation from a stronger investigator or by a capability gap, so it adds a self-investigation control.
quote: when a much more capable model runs the investigation, an uplift in the trained target may simply reflect distillation from the larger model, rather than anything specific to the training-data setup.
title: Training Models to Predict and Explain Their In-the-Wild Behavior

claim: Prefers a controlled cross-model test (privileged access) over assuming introspection because a model may merely learn a good prior over what the model tends to do.
quote: The model may be gaining some form of introspective privileged access to its own processing, or it may simply be learning a good prior over what this model tends to do, which any capable model could in principle learn from the same data.
title: Training Models to Predict and Explain Their In-the-Wild Behavior

claim: Limits claims to what was verified, restricting evaluation to counterfactual outcomes since open-ended explanation correctness is fuzzy, and avoiding the introspection label when the evidence doesn't support it.
quote: We therefore use the term "self-explanation" to describe the task format of training a model to report on its own behavior, and not as a claim that the skill is introspective.
title: Training Models to Predict and Explain Their In-the-Wild Behavior

claim: Uses an independent judge checking each explanation against the full experimental record, and includes negative evidence (hypotheses that failed) in reports, to make evidence more convincing.
quote: An independent judge verifies each explanation against the full experimental record.
title: Training Models to Predict and Explain Their In-the-Wild Behavior

claim: Treats weak or null results honestly, reading them as possible evidence that training struggles to elicit uniquely model-accessible information, while noting surprise and uncertainty.
quote: Together, these results suggest that training struggles to elicit information which is uniquely available to the model itself.
title: Training Models to Predict and Explain Their In-the-Wild Behavior

claim: Proposes using the datasets as a testbed and directly RL-ing against the counterfactual simulatability metric as future work.
quote: We think datasets such as ours are a promising testbed for future self-explanation methods (a natural direction is to directly RL against the counterfactual simulatability metric).
title: Training Models to Predict and Explain Their In-the-Wild Behavior
